newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD says jobs crisis threatens social order.
newsitem.headline: German SPD says jobs crisis threatens social order.

text.p: Germany's Social Democratic (SPD) opposition said on Thursday that data showing another rise in unemployment meant the country was entering the new year facing the worst jobs crisis since the 1930s.
"Mass unemployment threatens social stability in Germany," SPD economics spokesman Ernst Schwanhold said in a statement.
New jobs figures for December showed that unemployment rose by 48,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.156 million -- a post-war record.

Unadjusted unemployment, the focus of a heated political debate in Germany, surged by 206,000 to 4.148 million to the highest ever level for the month of December. Federal Labour Office head Bernhard Jagoda said he did not rule out this figure rising to a record 4.5 million in the near future.
Schwanhold hit out at Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government over pursuing tax cuts and making it easier to fire workers instead of taking action to create jobs.

"Germany needs an offensive for growth and jobs," Schwanhold said. He added that Kohl should take over personal responsibility for securing social stability and jobs from his Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt.
"The government has no ideas and is making vague promises," Schwanhold added. Kohl's government is struggling to hold on to a pledge to halve unemployment by the turn of the millenium.

Schwanhold also called on the Bundesbank to make a big cut in its leading interest rates to pull Germany out of its "historic jobs crisis". Interest rates at one percent would give the right signal to investors, he said.

The Bundesbank was due to decide on Thursday whether to change interest rates, but economists polled by Reuters said they expected no move. The discount rate is now 2.5 percent, the Lombard rate 4.5 percent and the repo rate three percent.
